[Diners: See dog and refuse to enter]

[Last Thursday, the measure allowing dogs to enter food premises officially came into effect. "Old Fung Tea House" (老馮茶居) at The Forest in Mong Kok is one of the dim sum restaurants permitted to allow dogs inside.]

[On that day (the 13th), a diner surnamed Fung requested to be seated "further away" upon being shown to her table. She was originally assigned to a table outside the designated area for guests with dogs, and was eventually seated in a corner of the restaurant, three to four tables away from the "dog zone." Ms. Fung said she would avoid restaurants with dogs if possible, fearing that some dog owners might not be disciplined enough to keep their dogs off the tables, and she was also worried about barking. She said she chose to dine here that day because she was with two elderly relatives, making it inconvenient to go elsewhere.]

[The restaurant's person-in-charge said the restaurant has already divided the dining areas for guests with dogs and ordinary guests. If a customer says they "won't enter if there are dogs," he said, "the customer has the right to choose."]

[Dog owners: Online discourse keeps amplifying isolated incidents]

[Ms. Chu and Ms. Au were diners who brought dogs, arriving at the restaurant that day with two Shiba Inus. Early on, both dogs repeatedly tried to nudge their noses close to the dining table, but Ms. Chu and Ms. Au blocked them with their hands and pushed the pet strollers further away to maintain distance from the table. When the server brought the dim sum to the table, the dogs showed no particular reaction and did not bark during the meal.]

[When Ms. Chu noticed diners "switching tables," she responded: "The current online discourse keeps grabbing one or two photos, amplifying them endlessly and making mountains out of molehills. That's not the reality—most dog owners are very disciplined."]

[Ms. Chu said she has actually run a pet-friendly café for six years and recently successfully obtained a licence to allow dogs into food premises. She said that when she goes to a cha chaan teng for a meal, she often hears neighbouring tables complaining about dogs. She believes many cha chaan tengs keep cats, which similarly have fleas, shed hair and produce waste—just that the public is less familiar with dogs. She said, "Right now we need to promote this issue, and we should come out even more to tell everyone it's fine."]

[Implementation varies greatly]

[Although the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department's guidelines state that food premises approved to allow dogs may set their own时段 and zones for dog entry as needed. From the 13th to the 17th, our reporters examined different premises approved to allow dogs and found striking differences: some allow dogs on seats, some only in pet strollers, and some only in outdoor areas.]

[The restaurant "Old Fung Tea House" sets each dining session at about one hour, admitting no more than four groups of customers with dogs per session. These customers are concentrated in a designated area separated by partitions from ordinary diners. Additionally, dogs are not allowed on the floor or on seats—they must remain in pet strollers and be held by hand throughout.]

[A staff member at "Hop Fat Cafe" (合發茶餐廳) on Canton Road in Mong Kok said small dogs may sit on seats, but large dogs, due to insufficient seating space, may only sit on the floor, where owners can hold them by hand or tie their leash to a table leg.]

[Meanwhile, "Kam Lung Cafe" (金龍冰室) on Kwong Fuk Road in Tai Po stipulates that customers with dogs may only be seated in the restaurant's outdoor area, with a maximum of three groups per session.]

[《Food Business Regulation》does not ban other animals]

[According to records, the 《Food Business Regulation》 only previously prohibited dogs from entering food premises. As for other animals, they were only barred from appearing inside food rooms such as kitchens; however, in areas outside food rooms, these animals were not prohibited—meaning pets such as cats and birds could enter areas outside the kitchen.]

[Different treatment for cats and dogs: law does not prohibit non-dog animals]

[A cat-themed restaurant in Mong Kok presents a stark contrast to the rules for dogs—not allowed on dining tables or bar stools. Cats in the restaurant can be said to roam freely.]

[Our reporter observed on-site that around 30-odd cats shared the space with five to six groups of diners, though the restaurant environment was spacious. As customers ate, cats jumped onto the dining tables, walked past their food, and meowed from time to time, with diners stroking the cats beside their plates while eating.]

[Meanwhile, at a cat café in Cheung Sha Wan, the café separates the cat area and the dining area into two rooms—meaning diners do not share a room with cats while eating. The café's person-in-charge said cats may eat things they shouldn't, which is why they separated the dining area to keep food away from the cats.]

[Why did the law previously only ban dogs?]

[Why did the law previously only ban dogs from food premises? According to records, in 2012, then Secretary for Labour and Welfare Matthew Cheung Kin-chung replied in writing to a question from then Legislative Council member Lau Kong-wah, who asked whether the authorities' prohibition on dogs entering food premises extended to other types of pets, and what the reasons were.]

[Government once cited dogs' close contact with humans as greater health risk]

[In his written reply, Cheung said that as domesticated animals, dogs are accustomed to close contact with humans. Allowing dogs into food establishments would pose a greater health risk to diners sharing the same space—particularly those with weaker constitutions or more susceptible to infection, such as the elderly, children, pregnant women or chronically ill patients.]

[More than a decade on, what prompted the government to amend the rules this time? The Food and Environmental Hygiene Department explained on its website that, in light of changing social norms, the government had reviewed multiple factors including public health safeguards, public acceptance, market demand, and industry feedback, and concluded that conditions were now in place to allow dogs into food premises under appropriate regulations.]
